# Chapter 11 Practice: Intermolecular Forces, Liquids, and Solids

*Auto-generated from the assessment guide (`assessment-support/intermolecular-forces.md`), grouped by objective. 15 questions spanning multiple-choice, short-answer, and workout formats.*

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 1
{{sp[info] Obj 11.1a}} · *multiple-choice* Which intermolecular forces are present in $\ce{CH3F}$ (fluoromethane)?

(A) Dispersion only
(B) Dipole-dipole and dispersion only
\(C) Hydrogen bonding, dipole-dipole, and dispersion
(D) Hydrogen bonding only
:::
::: tab Answer
**(B)** Fluoromethane is polar (C–F bond), so dipole-dipole and dispersion forces apply. However, its hydrogen atoms are bonded to *carbon*, not to F, N, or O — hydrogen bonding requires H bonded directly to one of those three atoms, which is not the case here.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 2
{{sp[info] Obj 11.1a}} · *short answer* Explain why $\ce{NH3}$ can hydrogen-bond with itself, but $\ce{PH3}$ (same group, one row down) cannot.
:::
::: tab Answer
Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded directly to N, O, or F — small, highly electronegative atoms. Nitrogen qualifies; phosphorus, despite being in the same group, is larger and less electronegative, so P–H bonds are not polar enough (and P is not small enough) to produce a hydrogen bond. $\ce{PH3}$ has only dipole-dipole and dispersion forces, which is why it boils at −87.7 °C versus $\ce{NH3}$'s −33.3 °C.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 3
{{sp[info] Obj 11.1b}} · *workout* Rank $\ce{Ne}$, $\ce{Ar}$, and $\ce{Kr}$ in order of increasing boiling point, and justify the order.
:::
::: tab Answer
All three are nonpolar monatomic noble gases, so only dispersion forces apply. Dispersion force strength increases with polarizability, which increases with the number of electrons: Ne (10 electrons) < Ar (18 electrons) < Kr (36 electrons).

$$\ce{Ne} < \ce{Ar} < \ce{Kr}$$

(Actual boiling points: Ne −246.1 °C, Ar −185.8 °C, Kr −153.2 °C — confirming the predicted order.)
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 4
{{sp[info] Obj 11.1b}} · *applied* Decane ($\ce{C10H22}$, nonpolar) boils at 174 °C, while hydrogen chloride ($\ce{HCl}$, polar) boils at −85 °C. Explain why the nonpolar substance boils at a much higher temperature.
:::
::: tab Answer
Boiling point depends on total intermolecular force strength, not on polarity alone. Decane is nonpolar and has only dispersion forces, but its large size and high electron count make those dispersion forces substantial — collectively stronger than HCl's smaller dipole-dipole + dispersion forces. This is the size/polarizability exception to the general polar-beats-nonpolar ranking.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 5
{{sp[info] Obj 11.2a}} · *short answer* Glycerin ($\ce{C3H8O3}$, with three O–H groups per molecule) is far more viscous than water at room temperature. Explain why.
:::
::: tab Answer
Each glycerin molecule can form multiple hydrogen bonds (three O–H groups vs. water's two), creating a more extensive hydrogen-bonding network per molecule. This stronger intermolecular attraction makes it much harder for glycerin molecules to slide past one another, producing much higher viscosity than water.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 6
{{sp[info] Obj 11.2a}} · *conceptual* In a thin glass tube, water rises above the surrounding liquid level, while mercury is depressed below it. What does this tell you about the relative strength of cohesion and adhesion for each liquid?
:::
::: tab Answer
For water: adhesion (water–glass attraction) exceeds cohesion (water–water attraction), so the liquid climbs the tube walls. For mercury: cohesion (strong metallic-like attraction between mercury atoms) exceeds adhesion (mercury–glass attraction), so the liquid pulls away from the walls and is depressed at the center.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 7
{{sp[info] Obj 11.2b}} · *short answer* Explain, at the molecular level, why ice is less dense than liquid water.
:::
::: tab Answer
In ice, each water molecule is locked into a rigid, hydrogen-bonded lattice that holds neighboring molecules at a fixed, relatively open (spacious) arrangement to maximize the number of hydrogen bonds. In liquid water, molecules are not locked in place and can pack somewhat more closely together on average. The more open solid structure gives ice a lower density than the liquid.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 8
{{sp[info] Obj 11.2b}} · *applied* Coastal cities generally have smaller day-to-night and summer-to-winter temperature swings than inland cities at the same latitude. Explain this in terms of one of water's anomalous properties.
:::
::: tab Answer
Water has an unusually high specific heat (4.184 J/g·°C) due to its extensive hydrogen bonding. Large bodies of water near coastal cities absorb or release large amounts of heat with only small temperature changes, moderating the surrounding air temperature and reducing extreme swings compared to inland areas without a large nearby water reservoir.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 9
{{sp[info] Obj 11.3a}} · *multiple-choice* Quartz ($\ce{SiO2}$) is best classified as which type of solid?

(A) Molecular
(B) Covalent network
\(C) Ionic
(D) Metallic
:::
::: tab Answer
**(B)** Every silicon and oxygen atom in quartz is linked by covalent bonds into one continuous three-dimensional network — there are no discrete molecules and no free-moving ions or delocalized metallic electrons. This gives quartz its characteristic hardness and very high melting point.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 10
{{sp[info] Obj 11.3a}} · *short answer* Diamond and graphite are both covalent-network forms of pure carbon, yet graphite conducts electricity and diamond does not. Explain the difference.
:::
::: tab Answer
In diamond, every carbon atom is $sp^3$-hybridized and forms four localized single bonds — all electrons are tied up in fixed bonds with nowhere to move, so diamond does not conduct. In graphite, each carbon is $sp^2$-hybridized, forming three bonds within a flat sheet plus a leftover, delocalized $p$ electron shared across the whole sheet. Those delocalized electrons are free to move, which is why graphite conducts electricity (well within its layers) despite being, like diamond, a covalent-network solid.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 11
{{sp[info] Obj 11.3b}} · *workout* How many atoms belong to one face-centered cubic (FCC) unit cell? Show the sharing-fraction arithmetic.
:::
::: tab Answer
FCC has 8 corner atoms and 6 face atoms.

$$\text{Corners: } 8 \times \frac{1}{8} = 1\ \text{atom}$$
$$\text{Faces: } 6 \times \frac{1}{2} = 3\ \text{atoms}$$
$$\text{Total} = 1 + 3 = 4\ \text{atoms per FCC unit cell}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 12
{{sp[info] Obj 11.3b}} · *inverse* A cubic unit cell has a coordination number of 8. Which cubic cell type is this, and how many atoms does it contain?
:::
::: tab Answer
Coordination number 8 identifies a **body-centered cubic (BCC)** cell (atoms touch along the cube's body diagonal). A BCC cell contains 2 atoms per cell (1 from the 8 shared corners, plus 1 full atom at the body center).
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 13
{{sp[info] Obj 11.4a}} · *workout* The molar heat of vaporization of ethanol ($\ce{C2H5OH}$, molar mass 46.07 g/mol) is 38.6 kJ/mol. How much heat is required to vaporize 25.0 g of ethanol at its boiling point?
:::
::: tab Answer
First convert mass to moles:

$$25.0\ \text{g}\ \ce{C2H5OH} \times \frac{1\ \text{mol}}{46.07\ \text{g}} = 0.543\ \text{mol}$$

Then multiply by the molar heat of vaporization:

$$0.543\ \text{mol} \times 38.6\ \text{kJ/mol} = 20.9\ \text{kJ}$$

**20.9 kJ** of heat must be absorbed to vaporize this sample.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 14
{{sp[info] Obj 11.4b}} · *workout* Water's vapor pressure is 23.8 mmHg at 25 °C, and its molar heat of vaporization is 40.66 kJ/mol. Use the Clausius–Clapeyron equation to estimate the temperature at which water's vapor pressure reaches 760 mmHg (i.e., estimate its normal boiling point).
:::
::: tab Answer
Using $\ln\left(\dfrac{P_2}{P_1}\right) = -\dfrac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_2} - \dfrac{1}{T_1}\right)$ with $T_1 = 298.15\ \text{K}$, $P_1 = 23.8\ \text{mmHg}$, $P_2 = 760\ \text{mmHg}$:

$$\ln\left(\frac{760}{23.8}\right) = 3.464 = -\frac{40{,}660}{8.314}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{298.15}\right)$$

Solving for $T_2$ gives $T_2 \approx 378\ \text{K} = 105\ \text{°C}$.

This is close to, but not exactly, water's true normal boiling point of 100 °C — the Clausius–Clapeyron equation assumes $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ is constant with temperature, which is only approximately true, so a few degrees of deviation from a single-$\Delta H_\text{vap}$ calculation is expected and normal.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 15
{{sp[info] Obj 11.4c}} · *short answer* Using the phase diagram of water, describe what happens if you start at a pressure of 0.5 kPa (well below atmospheric) and slowly raise the temperature from −20 °C, keeping pressure fixed at 0.5 kPa.
:::
::: tab Answer
At 0.5 kPa (about 0.005 atm), this pressure is close to but just below the triple-point pressure (0.00604 atm ≈ 0.612 kPa). Starting in the solid region and raising temperature at this low, roughly triple-point-adjacent pressure, water sublimes directly from solid to vapor without passing through a liquid phase — because 0.5 kPa is below the pressure needed to stabilize liquid water at any temperature along this path.
:::
::::
